newsitem.title: BERMUDA: Commonwealth demands more help to solve debt burden.
newsitem.headline: Commonwealth demands more help to solve debt burden.

text.p: Commonwealth finance ministers wound up three days of talks on Thursday demanding quick help for debt-strapped poor countries.

The ministers, representing about a quarter of the world's population and several of its poorest countries, also pressed for tighter controls on the flow of criminal money and for the encouragement of legitimate capital inflows to prime their economies.

"(Ministers) underscored the need for more realistic and flexible eligibility criteria (for debt relief), shortening of the waiting periods and equitable burden-sharing among multilateral institutions and bilateral creditors," they said in a statement at the end of talks on this Caribbean island.

Debt among developing countries has been a persistent theme at the meeting, with ministers arguing that the rules so far proposed to provide relief are so inflexible that few countries can hope to benefit soon.
It is also certain to be a dominant issue at next week's annual meeting in Washington of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund.
British Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke said he would press other wealthy nations to find an agreement to settle the problem.

"Everyone is committed to resolving this issue if we possibly can at next week's meeting. There is no-one arguing against the need to produce a result of this kind. I hope the preparatory work has got us all near enough to come to a satisfactory solution next week," he told reporters.
But it is looking unlikely that one of the key elements, the sale of some IMF gold to finance any bail-out as proposed by Clarke, will be agreed in Washington.
"I am not expecting that we will get down to details of...how much gold will be sold and when," Clarke said.
The ministers said they realised it was important for developing countries to get their own economic house in order as well as seeking help outside.
But they urged the IMF and World Bank to be more sensitive in the way they pressed governments to reform.
The ministers pressed for controls to end criminal money-laundering in the Commonwealth, which is home to several tiny island tax havens.
"Money launderers are criminals. They must be stopped in their tracks, caught and punished," Clarke said. "(It) poses a serious threat to every Commonwealth member."
"Unless we take effective action to deter and punish money laundering, serious crime...will remain an attractive business proposition to criminals," he said.
